As of 425 PM Tuesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1... As a cold front approaches on Wednesday and 
Wednesday night, showers and storms will become more widespread 
across the northern Piedmont and northern Coastal Plain. Excessive 
rainfall and flash flooding will be possible, and Flood Watches may 
need to be issued. Locally damaging winds also can't be ruled out.

Confidence is moderate-to-high for showers and storms to increase in 
coverage across the northern Piedmont late this evening into early 
Wednesday morning. A cold front pushing down slowly from Virginia 
will stall near the North Carolina border overnight, bringing a risk 
of continuous rainfall, which can be heavy at times, to the areas 
along and south of the NC border around daybreak. While an isolated 
severe storm with damaging wind gusts can't be ruled out tonight, 
the main concern will shift into Wednesday.

As mid/upper troughing with embedded shortwave impulses remains in 
place across the Eastern US on Wednesday, a strong cold front will 
approach and then slowly begin to cross the NW Piedmont on Wednesday 
night. While widespread cloud cover through the day will limit 
daytime heating across the north, models still show weak to moderate 
instability (up to 1000-1500 J/kg of CAPE) there. Above-normal PW 
values of 2-2.5 inches will also prevail ahead of the front, owing 
in large part to highly anomalous moisture being drawn in from the 
circulation of Tropical Storm Bertha over the northern Gulf.

CAMS generally show a band of showers and storms associated with a 
prefrontal trough that is mainly concentrated near the NC/VA border 
on Wednesday morning. This band will increase in coverage and 
intensity as it sags SE into the northern/western Piedmont and 
northern Coastal Plain in the afternoon and evening, continuing into 
the overnight hours. However, timing of this band is still somewhat 
uncertain, as it has slowed down in guidance like the GFS and NAM 
compared to the last couple days. If the 12z NAM Nest is accurate it 
won't really get going across our north until the evening and 
overnight hours, while the south stays mostly dry. So will have to 
watch is this trend continues. 

Regardless, once the band does set up, excessive rainfall is looking 
increasingly likely given the very moist air mass and strong signal 
for storm training, as the mean flow is from the WSW (roughly 
parallel to the front). WPC QPF is in the 1-2.5 inch range across 
our far northern counties, but HREF LPMM depicts potential for 3-5+ 
inches in localized spots. Some of these areas have already received 
1-3 inches over the last 2 days. Thus after internal collaboration 
with WPC, they are issuing a moderate (level 3 of 4) risk for 
excessive rainfall in our far NE Piedmont and northern Coastal Plain 
near the VA border for Wednesday and Wednesday night. Elsewhere, a 
slight (level 2 of 4) risk is in effect. Flood Watches may 
eventually be needed for parts of our area as well. Forecast 
rainfall amounts through Wednesday night quickly decrease to the 
south, with the 12z HREF mean depicting around a quarter inch or 
less in our southernmost tier of counties.

Furthermore, deep-layer shear of 30-40 kts across our northern 
counties could result in some organized storm cells/clusters that 
become strong to severe in the afternoon and evening. Thus most of 
central NC outside of the south is under a slight (level 2 of 5) 
risk for severe weather. Damaging winds will again be the main 
threat, and while 0-1 km SRH looks limited, an isolated tornado 
can't be totally ruled out.


KEY MESSAGE 2... Widespread showers and storms with a risk for 
flooding will continue into at least Friday and possibly even this 
weekend, particularly in our south and east, as a cold front stalls 
near the NC/SC border.

The cold front will move only slightly south and east on Thursday, 
and with rich Gulf moisture continuing to funnel NE along the front, 
another day of heavy rainfall and possible flash flooding is 
expected, this time across all of central NC. WPC QPF is 1-2 inches 
on average across the region, but this time the heaviest rainfall 
axis is shifted a bit SE. Once again, locally higher amounts will be 
possible. Thus after internal collaboration, WPC is also issuing a 
moderate (level 3 of 4) risk for excessive rainfall across eastern 
NC that includes some of our Coastal Plain counties, with a slight 
(level 2 of 4) risk for most of the rest of central NC. 

This threat for heavy rainfall unfortunately looks to continue 
across at least our SE zones on Friday and possibly even Saturday as 
the cold front stalls or drifts very slowly south somewhere near the 
NC/SC border. WPC QPF from Friday into Saturday depicts another 1-3
